summary:
Farmers often apply water and fertilizer uniformly across a field even though soil properties vary 
from one zone to another, and fruit is frequently lost after harvest during storage and transport. 
This project proposes an integrated, staged system to support more precise farm decisions. A 
wheeled robot visits a grid of measurement points, records soil salts, moisture, and 
temperature, and tags each reading with its grid location. The data is sent to a web platform 
that builds a soil map, combines it with climate and weather data and a crop-requirements 
database, and recommends suitable crops or evaluates a crop chosen by the farmer, with 
reasons and limitations shown. Later stages add a seed-metering mechanism for controlled 
spacing and depth, and a variable-rate fertilizer concept that begins as recommendations only. 
Separately, the project will test an active-packaging unit (for example, an ethylene absorber 
with temperature and humidity logging) on one fruit type against conventional storage.

Smart Farm: An Integrated AI-Powered Precision Agriculture and Food Preservation System

Smart Farm is an integrated agricultural technology project designed to address major challenges throughout the agricultural production cycle, including soil degradation, water scarcity, inefficient crop selection, and post-harvest food waste. The project combines a mobile soil-monitoring robot, a climate-informed agricultural decision-support website, AI-assisted plant disease screening, and an intelligent active packaging solution called Banana Shield.

1. How Does the Project Work?

A. Smart Soil-Monitoring Robot

The first component is a mobile agricultural robot designed to collect soil measurements from different locations across a farm. The robot is powered by an ESP32 microcontroller and equipped with two primary sensors:

  • Soil Moisture Sensor: Measures soil moisture levels to help identify variations in water availability and potential irrigation requirements.
  • TDS Sensor: Measures the concentration of dissolved solids in a prepared soil-water extract, providing an indirect indication of possible soil salinity.

The ESP32 processes the sensor readings and displays the measurements on an LCD screen. The system is designed to organize measurements according to agricultural zones, allowing farmers to identify differences in soil conditions across their land.

B. Smart Farm Website: NASA Climate Data and Agricultural Decision Support

The website is the central information and decision-support platform of the project. It connects soil measurements with geographical and climate information to provide farmers with a more comprehensive understanding of their agricultural land.

One of its most important features is its integration with NASA POWER (Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resources), a NASA data service that provides globally available solar and meteorological information for agricultural and other applications.

The website allows users to enter a city, select a location, or provide geographical coordinates. It then uses the location to retrieve relevant climate information from NASA POWER.

The climate information can include:

  • Average air temperature.
  • Maximum and minimum temperatures.
  • Precipitation levels.
  • Relative humidity.
  • Solar radiation.

These variables are important because they influence crop development, irrigation requirements, evapotranspiration, and the suitability of different crops under particular environmental conditions.

The website organizes climate information into visual charts and summaries, allowing farmers to understand seasonal climate patterns and compare environmental conditions between locations.

An important feature is the distinction between historical climate information and weather forecasts. NASA POWER provides historical, climatological, and near-real-time datasets rather than a guaranteed three-month weather forecast. These datasets can help establish seasonal climate expectations, while future weather forecasts can be incorporated separately when available.

The platform is designed to cover agricultural locations globally, including Egyptian cities and other international locations, using geographical coordinates rather than relying exclusively on a predefined list of cities.

C. Agricultural Land Assessment and Crop Recommendation

Smart Farm also aims to assist people who already own agricultural land as well as those considering purchasing land for farming.

Users can enter information about their location, soil conditions, available water resources, and agricultural objectives. The website combines these inputs with climate information to support the evaluation of potential crops.

The platform is designed to divide agricultural land into 256 individual zones, creating a more detailed representation of variations within a farm.

For each zone, the system can organize available soil and climate measurements and compare them with the environmental requirements of different crops.

The objective is to recommend crops that are more compatible with the available conditions rather than applying the same agricultural decision to the entire field.

The platform also aims to provide information about irrigation considerations, soil limitations, and factors that should be investigated before purchasing agricultural land.

D. AI-Assisted Plant Disease Screening

Another website feature allows farmers to upload photographs of potentially affected plants.

An AI-based image classification model analyzes the uploaded photograph and identifies possible plant disease categories. The platform can then present preliminary results and relevant agricultural recommendations.

This feature is intended to make plant-health information more accessible, especially to farmers who may not have immediate access to agricultural specialists. Its predictions are treated as preliminary screening results rather than confirmed diagnoses.

E. Banana Shield: Intelligent Active Packaging

The project also addresses agricultural losses after harvesting through Banana Shield, an intelligent active packaging concept designed to investigate methods of preserving fruit quality.

The proposed packaging consists of a cardboard box lined with aluminium foil, alongside additional materials with specific preservation purposes:

  • Aluminium foil provides a protective barrier.
  • Silica gel is intended to help manage moisture.
  • Charcoal is included as an intended ethylene-absorbing component.
  • A smart indicator is incorporated to monitor relevant storage conditions, depending on the final indicator design.

The packaging will be evaluated experimentally by comparing fruit stored in Banana Shield with fruit stored in conventional packaging. Parameters such as mass loss, firmness, visible deterioration, and storage conditions will be monitored to determine whether the proposed design provides measurable preservation benefits.

2. Tools, Technologies, and Materials

The project combines hardware, software, environmental datasets, and physical materials.

Hardware:

  • ESP32 microcontroller.
  • Soil moisture sensor.
  • TDS sensor.
  • LCD display.
  • Robot chassis and movement components.
  • Electrical connections and power supply.

Software and Programming:

  • Python for backend development and data processing.
  • Flask for the website backend and API communication.
  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the website interface.
  • SQLite for organizing and storing agricultural measurements.
  • AI-based image classification for preliminary plant disease screening.
  • NASA POWER API for retrieving geographical solar and meteorological data.

Banana Shield Materials:

  • Cardboard packaging.
  • Aluminium foil.
  • Silica gel.
  • Charcoal.
  • Smart storage-condition indicator.

3. Creativity and Innovation

The main innovation of Smart Farm is its integration of technologies that address different stages of agriculture within one connected system.

Traditional soil-monitoring approaches generally focus on collecting individual measurements, while climate information and post-harvest preservation are often considered separately.

Smart Farm connects these areas through a shared agricultural platform.

Its combination of mobile soil measurements and NASA-derived climate information provides a broader basis for agricultural decision-making. Instead of evaluating soil conditions independently, the platform is designed to interpret them alongside geographical and environmental factors.

The 256-zone approach adds another level of precision by recognizing that soil conditions can vary within the same farm. The AI-assisted plant screening feature extends the platform to plant-health monitoring, while Banana Shield addresses the separate challenge of preserving harvested produce.

This integration creates a system that considers agricultural decisions from land assessment and crop selection to plant monitoring and post-harvest preservation.

4. Factors Considered During Development

The team considered several factors when developing the project:

  • Water scarcity: The importance of monitoring soil moisture to support more informed irrigation decisions.
  • Soil degradation and salinity: The need to identify variations in soil conditions that may affect crop growth.
  • Climate variability: The importance of using geographical and climate datasets when evaluating crop suitability.
  • Accessibility: Designing a platform that can be used by farmers without requiring advanced technical knowledge.
  • Affordability: Selecting accessible electronic components and practical packaging materials.
  • Scientific reliability: Recognizing the importance of sensor calibration, standardized measurements, and experimental validation.
  • Environmental sustainability: Considering water efficiency, agricultural productivity, and post-harvest food waste.
  • Scalability: Designing the website around geographical coordinates so that the system can be applied beyond a single farm or city.

5. Benefits and Intended Impact

Smart Farm aims to support more efficient agricultural resource management by helping farmers understand their soil conditions, evaluate local climate characteristics, and make more informed crop-selection decisions.

Its intended benefits include supporting better irrigation planning, identifying possible soil-salinity concerns, improving access to agricultural information, and investigating practical approaches to reducing post-harvest fruit losses.

The project is particularly relevant to Egypt and other regions experiencing water scarcity, agricultural land degradation, and food-security challenges. However, its geographical design and use of NASA's global climate datasets give it potential applications in agricultural communities worldwide.

Ultimately, Smart Farm aims to demonstrate how Earth science data, robotics, artificial intelligence, and sustainable material design can work together to support more informed agricultural decisions and a more sustainable food system.
